title: Host facts
description: What was observed about a host, in the shape the core reads it. This is the contract a collector has to produce: gather runs against a machine and writes this document, and everything downstream reads the normalized model built from it, so a change in how facts are collected cannot ripple into the gate engine or the planner. Nothing here is a judgement. The collector reports what it saw, including which packaging family the operating system belongs to, because a distribution-to-family map living in the core would be exactly the kind of knowledge that has to stay out of it.

schema_version.description: The version of this contract. A collector and the core have to agree about it, so it is stated rather than inferred from which fields happen to be present.

collected_at.description: UTC, to the second. Facts have a shelf life: apply re-checks that the host still matches the ones its plan was built from.

host.description: The host as it was addressed, which is how a plan and a report name it afterwards.

arch.description: The processor architecture. Both spellings of the same machine are accepted here and resolved on the way in, because which of amd64 and x86_64 a collector happens to report is not something a collector should have to know this project's opinion about. Only the canonical spelling reaches a rule.

mounts.description: Every mounted filesystem, not only the interesting ones. Which mount carries a planned path is worked out by matching the longest prefix, and that answer is only right if the list is complete.

services.description: What is already installed and running. May be empty, which is the usual answer on a machine that has just been built. Whether any of it conflicts with what is being provisioned is a question the profile answers, not this document.

items.description: A locale as the host names it, so that a required one can be looked for exactly rather than approximately.

locales.description: The locales present on the host. An engine initialized with a locale the machine does not have fails at the last possible moment, so this is checked at the first.

items.description: A package repository URL the host answered from, spelled exactly as the profile spells it, so that the two can be compared rather than approximately matched.

reachable_repositories.description: The package repositories the host proved it can reach. Which ones were tried comes from the profile, so this is the one part of the facts that is collected knowing what is being provisioned. Absent means nobody asked, and the rule that reads it is skipped; present and empty means the host was asked and reached nothing, which is a refusal.

family.description: The packaging family, as the collector reports it. The core never derives this from the distribution: that map is knowledge about operating systems, and it belongs where the observation is made.

version.description: The version as the distribution writes it, quoted so that 24.04 stays two numbers and a dot.

codename.description: The release codename, where the family keys its repositories by one.

cores.description: Physical cores. Sizing that divides by this wants cores and not threads, because two threads on one core do not do twice the work.

total_bytes.description: Installed memory, in bytes. Sizing is written against this rather than against what happens to be free right now, because a plan has to hold for the life of the instance.

path.description: Where the filesystem is mounted. A drive letter is accepted because Windows targets are in scope, and a contract is cheaper to widen before anything depends on it.

filesystem.description: The filesystem type, as the host names it. Whether it is one the engine is normally run on is the profile's judgement, not this document's.

rotational.description: Whether the underlying device spins. Absent means it could not be determined, which is a different answer from false and is reported as such rather than guessed.

options.description: Mount options. A planned path on a read-only mount is a refusal, and this is where that is visible.

listening_ports.description: What is already listening. May be empty. A port that is taken is a refusal with a reason, rather than a service that fails to start after everything else succeeded.

protocol.description: Which protocol the socket is bound with. A port is only taken for the protocol it is taken on.

name.description: The unit or package name as the host knows it. It is matched against what a profile declares, never recognised by the core.

state.description: Running, stopped but present, or installed without a unit. A stopped instance still owns its data directory, so it counts as present.

user.description: The account the facts were collected as. A dedicated technical account, never a personal one.

can_escalate.description: Whether that account can run the privileged operations apply needs. Discovering it cannot, halfway through an install, is the outcome this fact exists to prevent.

synchronized.description: Whether the clock is actually in step, not merely whether a daemon is running. A database whose clock jumps is a database whose logs cannot be read against anything else.

swappiness.description: How readily the kernel swaps. A database that gets swapped out is a database that has stopped answering.

transparent_hugepages.description: The transparent huge page setting. Always is the one that causes latency spikes nobody can explain from inside the database.

open_ports.description: Ports the firewall already allows. An active firewall that does not admit the planned port is a warning, because opening it may be someone else's decision.
